content_voiceover: This slide builds the protein C anticoagulation pathway, one of the body's major natural brakes on clot formation. On the endothelial surface, thrombomodulin sits in the membrane and captures free thrombin, shown here as the small green T. Binding to thrombomodulin completely changes thrombin's personality, switching it from a clot-promoting enzyme into an anticoagulant one. Meanwhile, protein C circulates in plasma and docks onto the endothelial protein C receptor, which presents it to the thrombin-thrombomodulin complex. That complex then cleaves protein C into activated protein C, or A P C, which is released from the receptor. Notice factors Va and VIIIa are still drawn faded on the right side of the slide, because activated protein C has not yet reached them. This first half of the pathway is entirely about generating the active enzyme; the next slide shows what A P C actually does once it gets there.
keypoints: Binding converts thrombin from procoagulant to anticoagulant
Protein C docks on EPCR for presentation
Thrombin-thrombomodulin complex activates protein C to APC
keypoint_voiceover: Remember this sequence for boards. Thrombin binds thrombomodulin, which flips its function from clotting to anticoagulation. Protein C is presented by the endothelial protein C receptor, and the thrombin-thrombomodulin complex activates it into A P C. This whole process happens right on the endothelial surface, keeping the anticoagulant response localized to sites of vessel injury.
